questions.q: What is a Kafka topic, at its core?
options: A named log — the thing producers write to and consumers read from
A single physical file that can never be split
A relational database table with a fixed schema
A temporary in-memory queue that disappears when the broker restarts
questions.explain: A topic is simply a named log; the interesting structure is in how it's split into partitions underneath.

questions.q: Why is a topic split into partitions?
options: Partitioning is the unit of parallelism — different partitions can live on different brokers and be read/written concurrently
Partitions exist only for cosmetic organization in the UI and have no effect on performance
A topic can only ever have exactly one partition
Partitioning removes the need for offsets entirely
questions.explain: Splitting a topic into partitions is what lets Kafka scale reads and writes across multiple brokers and consumer group members.

questions.q: What ordering guarantee does Kafka actually make?
options: Ordering is guaranteed within a single partition, never across an entire topic
Ordering is guaranteed across the entire topic at all times
Kafka makes no ordering guarantees anywhere, ever
Ordering is guaranteed only between different topics
questions.explain: Two events in the same partition are strictly ordered; events in different partitions have no relative ordering guarantee.

options: A partition-local, increasing integer identifying an event's position — unique within that partition, not across the topic
A globally unique ID shared across every partition in a topic
The total number of partitions a topic has
A timestamp marking when the topic was created
questions.explain: Offset 500 in partition 0 and offset 500 in partition 1 are two unrelated events — offsets are local to their partition.
